basic_info.basic_info: Route/location proximity means arranging a date's stops so they are physically close together and flow in a single direction (a linear or loop path), minimizing back-and-forth travel, transit waiting, and re-navigation between stops. The goal is to reduce physical fatigue and 'dead' transition time so more of the date's energy and attention goes into shared experience rather than logistics. Unlike relationship-stage matching (which tunes emotional intensity) or venue quality (which picks good individual places), this is a spatial-logistics factor: it optimizes the connective tissue between stops, not the stops themselves. It also differs from simple duration control because two courses of equal length can feel very different depending on how much of that time is spent in transit versus in experience.

rationale.psychology: Several mechanisms make proximity matter. (1) Decision fatigue / ego depletion (Baumeister et al., 1998): every transfer forces micro-decisions — which exit, which direction, is this the right bus, where do we eat next — and self-control and choice quality draw on a shared, depletable resource; a low-friction, pre-sequenced route spares that budget so partners stay warm, patient, and present rather than irritable (note: the resource model of ego depletion has faced replication challenges, so treat this as a plausible rather than settled mechanism). (2) Transition/transaction cost and the perception of travel as 'dead time': long or awkward inter-stop travel is often experienced as wasted, breaking immersion and momentum; transport research on 'worthwhile travel time' (Mokhtarian and colleagues) shows travel is only tolerable when it carries enjoyment, productivity, or fitness value — a cramped, silent transfer usually has none, so shortening it or making it walkable (side-by-side, something to notice together) converts dead time into shared-experience time. (3) Peak-end rule (Kahneman): fatigue and logistical friction near the end disproportionately damage the remembered experience, so minimizing travel late in the course protects the ending. (4) Physical fatigue directly lowers mood and cognitive warmth, reducing the quality of conversation and affection. Walking dates specifically benefit from side-by-side positioning and a shared route, which lowers pressure and gives a natural conversational rhythm. Note: the direct causal link between reduced date-travel and higher date satisfaction is inferred from adjacent research rather than measured in dating-specific studies.

application.how_to_apply: Step 1 — Pick an anchor and build outward: choose one central venue, then select every other stop within a short walk (ideally under 10-15 minutes / roughly 1 km) of it or of the previous stop. Step 2 — Sequence as a line or loop, not a star: order stops so you always move forward in one direction, ending near the exit point (station, parking, or one person's route home) rather than doubling back. Step 3 — Cluster by neighborhood: prefer walkable districts where cafe, meal, activity, and dessert coexist, so the whole course is one connected zone. Step 4 — Make unavoidable travel 'worthwhile': route walks through pleasant, interesting streets (something to notice together) rather than dull or noisy stretches, turning transit into part of the date. Step 5 — Front-load any longer travel: if one leg must be far, put it early when energy is high, and keep late-course transfers minimal to protect the peak-end. Step 6 — Pre-plan and pre-decide the path (map it, note walking times, have a fallback) to remove in-the-moment navigation decisions and spare decision-making energy. Step 7 — Cap total walking/transit for the audience: keep cumulative travel comfortable (e.g., avoid heavy walking in formal shoes or bad weather) and include a sit-down midpoint.
application.common_mistakes: Star-shaped routing: picking individually great venues scattered across the city so the couple repeatedly returns to a hub or crisscrosses, spending more time in transit than together. Backtracking: ending far from where you need to disembark, forcing a tiring reverse trip. Underestimating transfer overhead: ignoring waiting, walking to/from stations, and parking, so a '20-minute' hop actually costs 40. Over-optimizing to the point of monotony: cramming everything so tightly that the course feels rushed with no breathing room — proximity should reduce fatigue, not eliminate pacing. Long travel late in the date, when fatigue is highest, damaging the remembered ending. Ignoring terrain, weather, and footwear when relying on walking. Choosing a 'convenient' route that is efficient but ugly/loud, wasting the chance to make transit itself enjoyable.
application.examples: Example 1 (linear walkable course): Coffee -> 8-minute walk through a pleasant main street -> lunch -> 5-minute walk -> exhibition -> 3-minute walk -> dessert, all within one neighborhood and ending one block from the subway — near-zero dead time, everything forward-moving. Example 2 (loop): Start and end at the same park entrance/station: rent bikes or walk a riverside loop hitting a viewpoint, a snack stand, and a cafe, returning to the origin so no separate return trip is needed. Example 3 (front-loaded travel): A daytime plan where the only longer ride (30 min to a scenic district) happens first while energy is high; the rest of the afternoon and the peak-end dinner all sit within a 10-minute walking radius so no tired late-night transfers spoil the finish.

evidence.evidence: Psychological basis: Decision fatigue / ego depletion — Baumeister et al. (1998); overview and replication caveats: Decision fatigue (Wikipedia) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_fatigue and 'Decision Fatigue: A Conceptual Analysis' (PMC) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6119549/ . 'Worthwhile travel time' framework (perceived value of travel as enjoyment/productivity/fitness) — https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01441647.2021.1983067 and 'Understanding worthwhile travel time' — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0965856424003847 . Peak-end rule — Kahneman (behavioral economics of remembered experience). Practical/applied sources: 'Walking Date Guide: Routes, Rules, and First-Date Tips' (GRASS) — https://grass.camp/en-US/blog/walking-date-routes-low-pressure-outdoor-dating ; 'Optimize travel transport: practical guide' (clustering by proximity, avoiding backtracking) — https://mytripflow.com/articles/how-to-optimize-travel-transport-within-an-itinerary/ ; Walkability definition — https://www.adventuresincre.com/glossary/walkability/ .
